hero.title: About this site
hero.tagline: The site as its own case study: how it was designed, the agents that maintain it, and how far it has come in a short time.

summary: The site you are reading. A resume-shaped evidence layer built from scratch, then handed a set of AI agent skills that tailor resumes, keep its documentation honest, and now carry its motion language. It started on June 28, 2026 and has not stopped moving.

bullets.text: Designed the Blueprint Press system: paper, ink, hairline rules, a fixed blueprint grid, and one easing curve shared by every transition, with ten palettes and a dark mode switchable from a local Studio.

Built a library of repository agent skills that generate job-targeted resume PDFs, keep an Obsidian vault in sync with the code, and distill a motion vocabulary from svelte-bits into this site's own restrained style.
Went from a single resume JSON to a data-driven Next.js site with a content editor, analytics, a social card, and a job-application tracker, deploying continuously the whole way.

caseStudy.title: RileyBeenders.com
caseStudy.subtitle: A portfolio that stays readable as a resume, and a workbench for the agents that maintain it
caseStudy.problem: A PDF resume is the document recruiters expect, but it flattens every project into two lines. I wanted a site that reads like that resume at rest and opens into the evidence behind each line, without turning into a marketing page.
caseStudy.rootCause: Early versions kept content, layout, and styling tangled in one file, so every visual change risked the content and every content change risked the layout. Splitting the data layer from the design, then giving each its own editor and its own agent procedures, is what let the site move fast without breaking.
constraints: Stay recognizable as a resume: no hero video, no marketing voice
Every claim on the site must trace to real work in the data files
Content edits must not require touching code
Motion must be subtle enough to survive a recruiter's ten-second scan
Ship continuously from a solo workflow
approach: Started from a scaffold in June and put a Coming Soon page live to learn deployment first
Split the resume JSON into focused files and merged them at build time
Designed Blueprint Press as a /v3 preview beside the old design, then promoted it and deleted the old one
Added a local Studio that edits the JSON with a schema-driven form and safe writes
Wrote repository agent skills for resume tailoring, vault sync, chart sync, and design tokens
Distilled a motion language from svelte-bits into three skills, then applied it here
designDecisions: One easing curve site-wide so every animation reads as the same hand
No pinning or scroll-jacking on the projects page; depth comes from parallax and a scroll-filled spine
Dark mode as a token swap on paper and ink, not a second design
The Studio runs outside the Next app on localhost only, so it can never be deployed by accident
Agent skills live in the repo as plain markdown so any tool can follow them, not just one
impact: Every project on the site is linked from a line of the resume, with a case study a click away
Content, palette, and typography change from a browser form with a byte-stable git diff
Tailored resume PDFs are generated from the same data the site renders
The vault documents the site well enough that an agent can pick up work cold

timeline.title: Genesis
timeline.summary: An interactive resume scaffold lands: one big resume JSON, a Next.js app, and a fixed lucide-react import. Nineteen files.

timeline.title: Coming Soon, and learning to deploy
timeline.summary: A holding page goes up so the deployment and reverse-proxy questions get answered before the design does.

timeline.title: The data split
timeline.summary: One JSON becomes a folder of focused files (header, summary, experience, skills, education, projects, proofs), merged at build time. Every later feature depends on this.

timeline.title: LIVE!
timeline.summary: V1.0 declared complete, a Download PDF button wired up, and the site goes public the same day.

timeline.title: First application submitted
timeline.summary: The reason the site exists starts working: the first job application goes out with a resume built from the same data, and the tracker begins.

timeline.title: The first agent instructions
timeline.summary: "Implemented AI": a SKILL.md tells any coding agent how to generate a tailored resume PDF from a job posting. The agent layer begins.

timeline.title: Version 2.0 on main
timeline.summary: Analytics, speed insights, and the application archive move onto main. The largest commit in the history by file count.

timeline.title: Sitewide update
timeline.summary: Version 2.1: a pass over every page while applications keep going out in the background.

timeline.title: The vault joins the repo
timeline.summary: An Obsidian vault documenting every route, component, data file, and pipeline is checked in, with a vault-sync skill that makes agents keep it current.

timeline.title: Blueprint Press previewed at /v3
timeline.summary: A new design direction: paper and ink, hairline rules, a blueprint grid texture, Instrument Serif and Spectral. Built beside the old design so both could be compared live.

timeline.title: Blueprint Press goes live, classic retired
timeline.summary: The new design is promoted to the root, the old one is deleted so the site has one set of URLs, and a favicon and social card land the same day.

timeline.title: Vault and agent rework
timeline.summary: One bundled SKILL.md is split into self-contained procedures, each matching its folder, with a README that routes between them.

timeline.title: Dark mode
timeline.summary: Paper and ink swap to navy and pale; everything else stays. A theme toggle in the nav, remembered per device.

timeline.title: The Studio
timeline.summary: A local, dependency-free content editor that reads and writes the data files through a schema-driven form, with backups, atomic writes, and conflict checks. The projects page is rebuilt alongside it.

timeline.title: Themes and fonts from the Studio
timeline.summary: Ten palettes plus custom colors, and three font roles, all chosen from a form and applied site-wide as CSS tokens.

timeline.title: Agent skills reworked
timeline.summary: Thirteen generic frontend-design skills are vendored in with a lock file, and every repo procedure is registered so any agent can find it.

timeline.title: Projects page: calm, then in motion
timeline.summary: The pinned, scroll-jacked project panel is replaced by an editorial flow, then given its motion: staggered bullets, media parallax, a scroll-filled spine, and photo wipes.

timeline.title: First project published
timeline.summary: ICARUS-Lite goes live with six photos and a full case study, and resume bullets gain reactive action words that take the accent on hover.

timeline.title: A motion language, and this page
timeline.summary: Three skills distilled from svelte-bits (what to animate, how to build it, how to compose it) are written, then used to build the page you are reading: the date bar, the timeline, the stats, the pins on the screenshots.

timeline.title: ExtrusionLine Studio
timeline.summary: The LabVIEW metrology project is written and hidden in the Studio, waiting on its two proofs (Modbus negotiation, hands-free start) before it publishes.

timeline.title: PROTEOR Print and the network
timeline.summary: Remote printer operations and the Ubiquiti network project follow, in the order the resume lists them.

timeline.title: The tracker returns
timeline.summary: The application timeline and table come back to More Info once the Studio can edit them, so the job search stays visible on the site that supports it.

timeline.title: Resume PDFs from the site itself
timeline.summary: The custom-resume skill already tailors a PDF per posting; the plan is to generate it from the site's own data at request time, so the download button is never stale.

pillars.title: Blueprint Press
body: The site is set on paper with ink, a red accent, and hairline rules, over a fixed blueprint grid you can see through the page. Headings are Instrument Serif, body is Spectral, and every transition on the site uses one easing curve so the motion reads as a single hand.

Dark mode swaps paper and ink to navy and pale and changes nothing else. Ten palettes and three font roles are chosen from the Studio and written as CSS tokens, so the whole system re-tunes from a form without a code change.
The projects page deliberately has no pinning or scroll-jacking. Depth comes from a media column drifting against the text, a spine that fills as you read, and photos that uncover bottom-to-top.

pillars.title: Skills in the repository
body: Standing instructions for any AI coding agent live in .agents/ as plain markdown, one folder per procedure, routed by a README. custom-resume builds a job-targeted PDF from a posting and the site's data. vault-sync keeps an Obsidian vault of 33 notes matching the code in the same session as any change. sync-charts keeps the application tracker identical in two places.
Thirteen generic frontend-design skills are vendored in with a lock file so drift upstream is detectable, and registered as first-class Claude Code skills.

The newest three, motion-design, motion-fluidity, and motion-layout, were distilled from the svelte-bits component library and translated into this site's system: numeric subtlety thresholds, a rated catalog of every effect, and copy-ready recipes. This entry is their first use.

pillars.title: A resume that shows its work
body: The PDF stays the official application document. The site is the evidence layer behind it: each line of the resume links to a project, and each project opens into the problem, the approach, and what changed.

Along the way the site became a hub for the search itself. Applications are tracked with tailored PDFs, and the vault holds a page per application comparing what the site claimed at the time against what it claims now.
Eighty-one days from a single JSON file to this. The timeline above is the honest version of that sentence.

backend.intro: None of this is on the live site. It runs on my machine and in the repository, and it is most of why the site can keep moving.

items.title: One posting in, one page out
body: The PDF is still the document that gets submitted. When I apply somewhere, an agent reads the posting, pulls the matching evidence out of the same data this site renders, and writes a one-page PDF in the site's format. Anything the data can't back up is left out, not softened.
The live Download PDF button on the home page is the same generator running on demand, so the resume on the site is never a stale file.
notes: Reads the posting PDF and data/**/*.json
Checks page count, links, and layout before delivery

matches.line: Built an automated LabVIEW QC system for real-time tolerance monitoring
Integrated a multi-board CAN-bus control architecture that simplified wiring and debugging
Designed and hosted a redundant Kubernetes cluster running a self-developed ERP/CRM
Researched high-speed linear motors moving a 30 kg payload at 3 m/s with 5-micron accuracy
Led the design and development of the ICARUS-Lite, owning mechanical, electrical, and software design

items.title: Edit the site from a form, not a code editor
body: Every word, image, palette, and font on this site comes from JSON files. The Studio is a small local editor that reads and writes them through a form built from a schema, so a content change never means opening a code file.
It only runs on this machine, backs up every save, and writes back byte-for-byte what it read plus the one thing that changed, so the git diff is just that change.
notes: Ten palettes plus custom colors, three font roles
Hidden projects keep their write-up until they publish
Never deployed: it is not part of the site

items.title: Standing instructions any agent can follow
body: The repository carries its own instructions for AI coding agents, written as plain markdown so any tool can follow them. Each one is a procedure I would otherwise have to remember: how to tailor a resume, how to keep the documentation honest, how motion on this site should feel.
They are the reason a fresh session can pick up work cold and still do it the way I would.
notes: Plain markdown in the repo, one folder per procedure
Registered as first-class skills so they trigger on ordinary requests
A vault of notes is kept current in the same session as any change

skills.name: custom-resume
skills.does: Reads the job PDF and the site's data, keeps only the claims the data supports, and writes a one-page PDF in the site's format.

skills.name: vault-sync
skills.trigger: Any change to the site's code, data, or config
skills.does: Updates the notes that describe the part of the site that changed, in the same session, before the task is done.

skills.name: sync-charts
skills.does: Keeps the tracker's chart and table identical in the two places they live.

skills.name: motion-design
skills.does: Decides what should move and how much, using a catalog of effects rated for this site's restrained style.

skills.name: motion-fluidity
skills.does: Builds it with the site's one easing curve and reduced-motion branch, from copy-ready recipes.

skills.name: site-timeline-sync
skills.does: Refreshes this page's numbers from git and adds only the commits that mattered to the timeline.
